source.title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.

accepted.question_text: For galaxies observed over a wide range of redshifts and halo masses, can astronomers reduce the systematic uncertainties involved in converting observed spectra or broadband photometry into stellar mass, meaning the total mass in stars, and star formation rate, meaning the rate at which stellar mass grows through star formation; or are standard methods reaching a fundamental limit in how accurately these quantities can be measured and used to improve galaxy-formation theory?
accepted.context_brief: Fundamental limits in measuring stellar mass and star formation rate

evidence.quote: Two of the most fundamental parameters that describe a galaxy are its total mass in stars, and the rate at which stellar mass grows via star formation, the star formation rate (SFR).
Can we really develop techniques to reduce systematic uncertainties in deriving key quantities such as stellar mass and SFRs, or are we truly reaching a fundamental limit in our ability to do so?

accepted.question_text: When galaxy stellar masses are inferred by fitting spectral energy distributions to synthetic spectra from stellar population synthesis models, how large are the true systematic uncertainties introduced by the choice of synthesis model, treatment of stellar-evolution phases such as thermally pulsing asymptotic giant branch stars, metallicity, initial mass function, star formation history, dust attenuation law, dust geometry, emission lines, stellar rotation, binary evolution, and other currently untested or missing ingredients?
accepted.context_brief: Systematic uncertainties in SED and SPS stellar-mass fitting

evidence.quote: Figure 1 shows that the largest systematic uncertainty in the determination of stellar masses for individual galaxies is the choice of SPS model, and this difference is a factor of ∼ 1.6.

However, these are simply varying the so-called ‘known unknowns’ and so realistically provide only a lower-limit on the size of systematic uncertainties given that there are certainly still ‘unknown unknowns’ in the process (e.g. if unusual IMFs or strange dust laws exist, the effect of these on deriving stellar masses has not been tested).
Currently, one of the most heavily debated issues in the SPS community is the treatment of the TP-AGB phase of stellar evolution.
Given the challenges of determining the IMF for any galaxies other than locally, the IMF may prove to be a fundamental limitation in our ability to measure stellar masses.

accepted.question_text: What are the star formation and assembly histories of galaxies with stellar masses below 10^9 solar masses, including gas-poor dwarf spheroidal galaxies concentrated around more massive galaxies and dwarf irregular galaxies with gas fractions ranging from nearly zero to one that tend to be more isolated?
accepted.context_brief: Star formation and assembly histories of low-mass galaxies

evidence.quote: Question 2 - What is the star formation and assembly history of galaxies with mass below 10^9 M⊙?

Galaxies with stellar mass below 10^9 M⊙ exhibit a variety of physical properties, from dwarf spheroidals (dSph) that are gas poor and tend to be concentrated around more massive galaxies, to dwarf irregulars (dIrr) whose gas fraction can vary from zero to one, and tend to be more isolated than dSphs.

accepted.question_text: What physical feedback, gas recycling, or gas-accretion mechanism can solve the low-mass galaxy problem in hierarchical and hydrodynamical galaxy-formation models, where models overproduce low- and intermediate-mass galaxies, make low-mass galaxies too old and passive, fail to reproduce the observed anti-correlation between specific star formation rate and stellar mass, and need to decouple late low-mass galaxy growth from the earlier growth of their host halos without overproducing cold gas?
accepted.context_brief: Physical mechanism behind low-mass galaxy model failures

evidence.quote: recent studies have pointed out the existence of a fundamental problem with the evolution of low mass galaxies in hierarchical galaxy formation models, as well as in the state-of-the-art hydrodynamical simulations
Models also fail to reproduce the observed anti-correlation between specific star formation rates and stellar mass.
what appears to be needed is a mechanism that is able to decouple the growth of low-mass galaxies (that occurs late) from that of their hosts (that, in contrast, occurs early).

Alternative scenarios that invoke suppression of gas accretion in low mass haloes can alleviate significantly the problem. Unfortunately, however, these scenarios appears to be ‘ad hoc’, and the exact mechanism remains unclear.
It remains to be seen if this can be achieved by modifying the stellar feedback scheme.

accepted.question_text: How can fully cosmological simulations form realistic rotationally supported disk galaxies with thin, high-angular-momentum stellar disks, rather than producing overly compact disks and large bulges through excessive early gas cooling and angular-momentum transfer from baryons to dark matter?
accepted.context_brief: Angular momentum and realistic disk-galaxy formation

evidence.quote: This produces a net and significant transfer of angular momentum from the baryons to the dark matter, resulting in spiral galaxies with large bulges and compact disks (this is the so called ‘angular momentum catastrophe’).
The formation of a realistic rotationally supported disk galaxy in a fully cosmological simulation is still an open problem.
Despite much progress, however, the formation of thin and high angular momentum stellar disks remains a challenge

accepted.question_text: How should age uncertainties in low-mass galaxies be understood and reduced so that star formation histories inferred from spectral energy distribution fitting, main sequence integration, and color-magnitude diagrams can be reconciled, especially when color-magnitude-diagram estimates suggest dwarf galaxies formed large fractions of their stars at redshifts greater than one?
accepted.context_brief: Age uncertainties in low-mass star formation histories

evidence.quote: But how well do we know the star formation and assembly histories of these low-mass galaxies?
The figure shows that estimates based on the CMD are largely inconsistent with those obtained extrapolating results based on SED-fitting techniques.
Given the strong constraining power of these observables, a better understanding of age uncertainties in this mass range is clearly needed.

accepted.question_text: Does dividing galaxies into central galaxies, defined as galaxies located at the centers of the most massive or dominant dark matter halos, and satellite galaxies, defined as galaxies in bound subhalos of more massive halos, provide the right framework for studying galaxy evolution across clusters, compact groups, Local-Group-like systems, and other environments?

evidence.quote: Question 3 - Does the central-satellite division provide the right framework to study galaxy evolution?

Galaxies that are located at the center of the most massive, dominant halo are defined as ‘central’ galaxies, and those that are in bound subhalos of more massive halos are defined as ‘satellite’ galaxies.
But how accurately can we correctly identify galaxies as either centrals or satellites?
Therefore it is possible that the central/satellite framework may be failing to capture the interesting effects of environment on the evolution of many galaxies.

accepted.question_text: For galaxy systems like the Local Group, where the Milky Way and M31 each have their own satellite populations but may be assigned to a single halo by group-finding algorithms, what physical information is lost by forcing the system into a single central-satellite hierarchy, how can that lost information be measured, and which lost information matters most for understanding galaxy evolution?
accepted.context_brief: Information loss in Local-Group-like central-satellite assignments

evidence.quote: The concern here is that we may be losing our ability to understanding the physics of galaxy evolution in systems similar to the Local Group if we are assigning the SMC and LMC satellites of M31, a galaxy that clearly does not dominate their future evolution.

The question that needs to be answered in a quantitative way is, what information are we really loosing by forcing systems like the Local Group into the central/satellite division? How can we know what information is lost? What is the most important information?

Both the Milky Way and M31 are centrals of a system of smaller satellites. However, many of the typical central/satellite algorithms when applied to the system would likely classify M31 as the central, and the Milky Way (and its satellites) as satellites of M31.

accepted.question_text: How do environmental processes such as ram-pressure stripping, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, and assembly bias combine through interacting actions, back-reactions, and self-regulation to produce the observed detailed trends in satellite galaxy properties, and how can the relative role of each physical process be quantified?
accepted.context_brief: Relative roles of environmental galaxy-evolution processes

evidence.quote: Question 4 - We understand which processes affect galaxies in different environments. Do the details matter?

we know which processes affect the evolution of satellite galaxies (ram-pressure, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, and assembly bias are all at work), we certainly do not understand how these processes combine to establish the detailed trends we observe.

Therefore, the obvious answer to this question is: yes, the details do matter because, in order to understand how galaxies evolve in different environments, we need to quantify the relative role of different physical processes.

accepted.question_text: What causes galaxy conformity, the observation that satellites appear to correlate with the star formation properties of their central galaxy, such that star-forming central galaxies have a higher fraction of late-type satellites than halos with early-type central galaxies?

evidence.quote: The central/satellite framework also revealed the puzzling issue of the ‘galaxy conformity’

Star-forming centrals have a significantly higher fraction of late-type satellites than haloes with an early-type central galaxy. As of yet, the reason for the galaxy conformity is not well understood.

accepted.question_text: How can satellite galaxies sustain significant star formation for several billion years after being accreted into larger halos and then quench rapidly enough to avoid producing too many galaxies with intermediate specific star formation rates, given that current models with instantaneous or gradual hot-gas stripping still decline too rapidly or fail to match observations?
accepted.context_brief: Satellite star formation persistence and rapid quenching

evidence.quote: active satellite galaxies form stars at a rate that is very similar to that of central galaxies of the same mass, suggesting that the transition from active to passive must be very rapid.
satellite galaxies must have evolved as central galaxies (forming stars at very similar rate) for several Gyrs

It remains unclear how satellite galaxies can sustain significant levels of star formation for several Gyrs, and if this can be achieved by simply relaxing the assumption of instantaneous stripping of the hot gas reservoir associated with galaxies when they are accreted.

accepted.question_text: For galaxy groups, which are likely the most common environments experienced by galaxies, how important are different environmental processes such as ram-pressure stripping, tidal effects, and evolution of gaseous components at typical group velocity dispersions, and to what degree do shortcomings in modeling these processes explain problems with satellite galaxy evolution?

evidence.quote: published work on the role of environment on galaxy evolution is still largely focused on massive galaxy clusters
groups likely represent the most common environment that galaxies experience

additional work on detailed controlled numerical experiments (including the evolution of the gaseous components) is needed in order to quantify the importance of different physical processes, at the typical velocity dispersions of galaxy groups.
This will also help us understanding to what degree the problem with satellite galaxies is related to a poor treatment of environmental processes.

accepted.question_text: How should next-generation galaxy-formation models be extended to exploit upcoming resolved spectroscopy, atomic hydrogen, and molecular-gas observations, including explicit treatment of the transition from atomic to molecular gas, possible modeling of spatially resolved physical properties, and detailed chemical evolution with abundance ratios as constraints?
accepted.context_brief: Model extensions for upcoming galaxy-evolution data

evidence.quote: In order to make the best use possible of the overwhelming amount of data that will come in the next future, our theoretical tools need to be updated including an explicit treatment of the transition from atomic to molecular gas, and (possibly) an explicit modelling of spatially resolved physical properties.
metals (including detailed abundance ratios) still represent a underutilized, yet very powerful constraint to models of galaxy formation and evolution
Therefore, the new generations of galaxy formation models and simulations should all include an explicit and detailed treatment of the chemical evolution of different species.
